extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate / graduate students and researchers in combinatorial & discrete geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and reasons about combinatorial-geometry definitions, structural properties, and proof-ingredients (slope problem, Euler's formula consequences, Pick's theorem, Cauchy rigidity, touching simplices). Focuses on the formal conditions used in these proofs and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence-of-permutations model for slopes
rubrics_metrics.description: A point configuration in the plane gives rise to a periodic sequence of permutations π0 → π1 → ... → πt where π0 = 123...n, πt = n...321, the length t equals the number of distinct slopes determined by the points, every pair i<j is switched exactly once, and every move reverses one or more disjoint increasing substrings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a starting projection direction not aligned with any slope (π0 = identity). Rotate direction by 180° to obtain πt = reverse. Changes occur exactly when direction passes a configuration slope, and each move corresponds to reversing disjoint increasing substrings (possibly several at once). This combinatorial model is the basis for counting/moving arguments in the slope problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crossing move (and order)
rubrics_metrics.description: A move πi → πi+1 is a crossing move if one reversed substring crosses the central barrier between left and right halves; its order d means it moves 2d letters across the barrier (d letters on one side and at least d on the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret geometrically as the direction of a line with fewer than m = n/2 points on each side. In the sequence, each label 1..n must cross the barrier at least once; if crossing moves have orders d1,...,dc then Σ 2di ≥ n. A single crossing of order  n/2 occurs only if all points are collinear (t=1). Examples and explicit permutations illustrate orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Touching move
rubrics_metrics.description: A touching move reverses a substring adjacent to the central barrier but does not cross it; geometrically it corresponds to a line whose slope places exactly m points on one side (and ≤ m−2 on the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Touching moves affect whether the barrier sits inside an increasing substring and are constrained in their placement relative to crossing moves. They are encoded as T in the T/O/C notation and are necessary between certain crossing moves (see embedding facts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary move
rubrics_metrics.description: A move that is neither crossing nor touching; it reverses an increasing substring fully contained on one side of the central barrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Denoted O in the T/O/C notation. Ordinary moves shorten a symmetric decreasing substring by at most one letter on each side; many combinatorial bounds count ordinary moves in relation to crossing/touching moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: T-O-C pattern embedding and crossing/touching spacing facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Key combinatorial facts: (i) Between any two crossing moves there is at least one touching move. (ii) Between a crossing move of order d and the next touching move there are at least d−1 ordinary moves. Also, running the sequence in the opposite direction implies: Between a touching move and the next crossing move of order d there are at least d−1 ordinary moves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These facts follow from the structure of symmetric decreasing substrings around the barrier and how touching moves are the only ones that can place the barrier into an increasing substring. They imply that each crossing move of order d is embedded in a local pattern T, O,...,O, C(d), O,...,O of total length 2d, and summing these yields t ≥ Σ 2di ≥ n, proving t ≥ n for t≥2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's formula for connected plane graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: If G is a connected plane graph with n vertices, e edges and f faces, then n − e + f = 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a spanning tree T of G (no cycles) and the dual graph G*: edges in T* correspond to E \ T and form a spanning tree of G*. For trees, vertices = edges + 1, giving n = e_T + 1 and f = e_T* + 1; adding yields n + f = e + 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertex-degree and face-counting identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard double-counting identities: n = Σ ni (ni = number of vertices of degree i), 2e = Σ i·ni; f = Σ fk (fk = number of k-sided faces), 2e = Σ k·fk. Average degree d = 2e/n; average face-sides = 2e/f.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret as counting edge-vertex and edge-face incidences in two ways. Use these identities repeatedly to derive numerical bounds and contradictions in planar-graph arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edge bound for simple planar graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: For any simple connected plane graph with n > 2, the number of edges satisfies e ≤ 3n − 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Since each face has at least 3 sides for simple graphs, 2e = Σ k·fk ≥ 3f, combine with Euler's formula to obtain 3n − 6 ≥ e. This is a standard necessary condition for planarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of a low-degree vertex in simple planar graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: Any simple plane graph with n > 2 has a vertex of degree at most 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From e ≤ 3n − 6 we get average degree d = 2e/n < 6, hence some vertex has degree ≤ 5. This is used in proofs like Sylvester–Gallai via dualization to find small-degree vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-color edge-change constraint at a vertex
rubrics_metrics.description: If the edges of a simple plane graph are two-colored, then there exists a vertex where the cyclic order of incident edges has at most two color-changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof counts corners where color changes occur (c) and uses face-counting bounds to derive 4n ≤ c ≤ 4e − 4f, contradicting Euler's formula if every vertex had ≥4 changes; thus some vertex has ≤2 changes. This local combinatorial constraint is applied in rigidity proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sylvester–Gallai theorem via Euler/duality
rubrics_metrics.description: For any finite set of n ≥ 3 points in the plane not all collinear, there is a line containing exactly two of the points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embed plane into sphere (points ↔ antipodal pairs), dualize to great circles. The arrangement gives a plane graph on S2 with all vertex degrees even and ≥4; by the low-degree vertex fact (degree ≤5) we obtain a vertex of degree 4, which corresponds to a great circle meeting exactly two antipodal pairs, giving the desired line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monochromatic line theorem (two-colored points)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any finite configuration of black and white points in the plane not all on one line, there exists a monochromatic line (a line containing at least two points of one color and none of the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dualize to colored great circles on S2. At a vertex where great circles of different colors intersect, part (C) implies existence of a vertex with at most two color-changes, yielding an intersection point that lies only on circles of one color — i.e., a monochromatic line in the primal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick's theorem (lattice polygon area formula)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any polygon Q ⊆ R^2 with integer-coordinate vertices, area A(Q) = n_int + (1/2) n_bd − 1, where n_int and n_bd count interior and boundary lattice points respectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use triangulation of Q into elementary triangles (vertices integral, no other lattice points). Lemma: every elementary triangle has area 1/2. Interpreting the triangulation as a plane graph and counting faces/edges/vertices via Euler yields the formula A = n_int + 1/2 n_bd − 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary triangle area lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Any elementary triangle (convex with integer vertices and no other lattice points) has area 1/2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form the parallelogram P = Δ ∪ σ(Δ) via center reflection; translations of P tile the plane and its area equals 1, so triangle area is 1/2. This underpins Pick's theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's rigidity theorem (convex polyhedra)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two 3-dimensional convex polyhedra P and P' are combinatorially equivalent and corresponding facets are congruent, then the dihedral angles between corresponding facets are equal, hence P and P' are congruent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color edges + if angle in P' is larger and − if smaller; project to sphere to get a two-colored plane graph on S2. By part (C) find a vertex with ≤2 sign changes; intersect with small spheres to get spherical polygons Q and Q' with equal side lengths but some angles opened/closed. Apply Cauchy's arm lemma to derive contradictions unless all dihedral angles match.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cauchy's arm lemma (polygon edge-length inequality)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Q and Q' are convex n-gons with corresponding edges equal for 1 ≤ i ≤ n−1 and corresponding interior angles satisfy αi ≤ α'i for 2 ≤ i ≤ n−1, then the distance between the first and last vertices satisfies q1 qn ≤ q'1 q'n, with equality iff all αi = α'i.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proved by induction on n (n=3 uses the cosine rule or spherical analogue). Used in the rigidity argument to show an increasing of internal angles (while preserving side-lengths) cannot decrease the 'missing' edge length, yielding contradictions under the ± sign pattern unless angles are identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and lower-bound construction for touching simplices f(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: f(d) denotes the maximum number of pairwise-touching d-simplices in R^d (pairwise intersections are (d−1)-dimensional). There exists a construction showing f(d) ≥ 2^d: for each d≥2 there is a family of 2^d pairwise-touching d-simplices together with a transversal line hitting the interior of every simplex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction uses an induction: start from d=2 (four triangles with a transversal); build a configuration with transversal line and then reflect/stack to obtain 2^{d} simplices in Rd. The transversal ensures interior intersections when combining reflected copies to move up in dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper bound for touching simplices: f(d) < 2^{d+1}
rubrics_metrics.description: For all d ≥ 1, the number r = f(d) of pairwise-touching d-simplices in R^d satisfies r < 2^{d+1}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate the s distinct facet hyperplanes H_j and choose halfspaces H_j^+ arbitrarily. Build the (r×s) B-matrix with entries in {+1, −1, 0} (row for each simplex, +1/−1 if simplex lies in chosen side of a facet hyperplane, 0 if facet not present). Each row has exactly d+1 nonzeros; rows differ pairwise in a column with +1 vs −1. Expand rows by substituting zeros with ±1 to get matrix C with 2^{s−d−1} r distinct ±1 rows; but there are at most 2^s distinct ±1 vectors, and at least one possible ±1 vector (coming from a point outside all simplices) is not represented, yielding strict inequality 2^{s−d−1} r < 2^s and hence r < 2^{d+1}.
